title: The Power of Examples and Non-Examples
author: Carl Hendrick
summary: Re-reading Engelmann and Carnine's 1982 Theory of Instruction against fifty years of subsequent learning research, Hendrick argues its central concept, "faultless communication", remains the most underrated idea in instructional design: teaching designed so precisely that misunderstanding becomes impossible. The mechanism is the disciplined pairing of examples with non-examples that differ only in the critical feature defining the concept, so that a non-triangle should be a four-sided shape rather than a cloud. He notes that the principle is unusually ecumenical, with Socrates, Aristotle, Vygotsky, Bruner, Skinner, Ausubel and Sweller converging on the claim that knowing what something is requires knowing what it is not. The piece then walks through Engelmann and Carnine's five principles: consistent wording to avoid distraction, setup so that examples differ only in the defining feature, consecutive presentation so contrasts are juxtaposed rather than separated, sameness through widely varied instances sharing a label, and a testing principle. Hendrick's closing argument is that Direct Instruction is the most misunderstood theory of learning, and that even teachers who reject scripted lessons and choral response should study its sequencing.
points: The operative discipline is that a non-example must be almost identical to the example, since arbitrary differences let students attach the concept to colour, shape or position instead of the defining feature.
Hendrick treats the convergence of Socrates, Vygotsky, Skinner, Ausubel and Sweller on contrast-driven concept formation as near enough to a unified theory of learning.
The difference principle requires juxtaposition: the same well-chosen pair loses its force when other items are interposed between them.
The sameness principle inverts the logic, using maximally varied instances under one label so learners see which observed differences are irrelevant to the concept.
He separates Direct Instruction's instructional design and sequencing from its delivery conventions, arguing the former is worth study even by teachers who reject scripting and choral response.
quotes: It's not an easy read but for me the core concept in it is "faultless communication": the idea that teaching should be designed so precisely that misunderstanding is impossible.
One key idea is that students learn faster when they see what something is and what it isn’t.
By that I mean cases that are deliberately chosen to contrast with examples, differing only in the critical feature that defines the concept being taught.

Socrates, Aristotle, Vygotsky, Bruner, Skinner, Ausubel, Sweller all basically say the same thing on this which is that learning is driven by clear distinctions—knowing what something is requires knowing what it isn’t.
A non-example should be almost identical to the example, differing only in the defining feature otherwise, students might focus on the wrong thing.
The Wording Principle: To keep instruction clear, teachers should use consistent or nearly identical wording across examples. This minimises distractions and helps students focus on key details.
Juxtaposition ensures that critical distinctions are immediately noticeable, reinforcing accurate concept formation.
